## 3. Does the Vacuum Boil in Quantum Field Theory? {#boiling-vacuum}

Popular accounts picture the vacuum state as constantly fluctuating, with particles appearing and disappearing. For some, this analogy helps to build an intuitive picture. Others are firmly against such an interpretation. Let us try to separate the myths from the mathematics.

### Is the vacuum "empty"? {#is-the-vacuum-empty .unnumbered}

No. The vacuum is the quantum state of lowest energy, and it carries nonzero correlations: $$\langle 0 | \hat{\phi}(x)\hat{\phi}(y) | 0 \rangle \ne 0$$ This means that the vacuum has a structure, expressed through the correlations of the field values at different points.

### Does the vacuum oscillate in time? {#does-the-vacuum-oscillate-in-time .unnumbered}

As a state vector, the vacuum is stationary: $$\hat{H} |0\rangle = E_0 |0\rangle$$ But the correlation functions of the fields depend on time: $$\langle 0 | \hat{\phi}(x^0, \vec{x}) \hat{\phi}(y^0, \vec{y}) | 0 \rangle \ne \text{const}$$ This is not classical "motion", but it points to an internal dynamics of the statistical properties.

### Can the vacuum be written explicitly in terms of the field operator? {#can-the-vacuum-be-written-explicitly-in-terms-of-the-field-operator .unnumbered}

No. The vacuum is not built explicitly out of the fields. It is specified by correlation functions, for example $$\langle 0 | \mathcal{O}[\hat{\phi}] | 0 \rangle$$ In the axiomatic approach it is treated as a positive linear functional on the algebra of field operators.

### Are there particles in the vacuum? {#are-there-particles-in-the-vacuum .unnumbered}

In the standard (non-accelerated) frame of reference, $$\hat{N} |0\rangle = 0$$ An accelerated observer, however, may interpret the vacuum as a thermal state with particles (the Unruh effect).

### Why do people say that "the vacuum fluctuates"? {#why-do-people-say-that-the-vacuum-fluctuates .unnumbered}

Because the variance is nonzero: $$\langle 0 | \hat{\phi}^2(x) | 0 \rangle - \langle 0 | \hat{\phi}(x) | 0 \rangle^2 \ne 0$$ This reflects the statistics of measurement outcomes, not the presence of classical dynamics or of processes in time.
